passage: On the 7:40 bus from Nandurbar, Vijay spotted Madhuri three seats ahead. They had been in the same class till tenth, and he hadn't seen her in six years. He half stood, then noticed: earphones in, eyes closed, forehead against the window, a thick file clutched on her lap. Her lips were moving as if she were going over something. An exam, maybe, or an interview. He sat back down. For forty minutes he watched the cotton fields go by and let her be. At the kasba stop she pulled out the earphones, stretched and looked around. That was his moment. "Madhuri? Vijay, from Sharda Vidyalaya." Her face opened into a grin. "Vijay! I just finished revising for my interview. Walk with me to the office?"

qa.q: What was Madhuri holding on her lap?
qa.a: She was holding a thick file.

qa.q: Why did Vijay sit back down instead of greeting Madhuri?
qa.a: He felt eager to say hello but hesitant to intrude, since her earphones, closed eyes and moving lips suggested she was busy revising.

qa.q: When was the right moment to start the chat, and why?
qa.a: At the kasba stop, when she took out her earphones and looked around, because she was now open to talk.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have felt if Vijay had interrupted her on the bus?
qa.a: She might have felt distracted and a bit annoyed before her interview, and the reunion would have been less warm.

grounding: Shows someone noticing another person's earphones and focus, holding off on a chat until she is open, and getting a warm reply.

passage: At the Kodungallur temple festival, Gopika sat alone on the steps of the pond, her leaf of payasam going cold. She had come with her hostel friends, lost them in the crowd an hour ago, and her phone had no signal. A young man with a volunteer badge sat down a careful distance away. "You look like you're waiting for someone. I'm Ramesh, I help at the food counter. Everything okay?" Relief washed over her, and right behind it, caution. She glanced at the badge, then at the families nearby. "I'm Gopika. I lost my friends. They said they'd be near the elephant stand." "The volunteer desk can announce their names. It's just there, by the big lamp." She nodded, then asked back, "Have you volunteered here long?" "Six years. My grandmother's idea." He pointed the way, and she walked to the desk herself.

qa.q: Where was the volunteer desk?
qa.a: It was just there, by the big lamp.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel when Ramesh sat down?
qa.a: She felt relief, and right behind it caution, so she checked his badge and the families nearby.

qa.q: What made Gopika's response both warm and sensible?
qa.a: She answered kindly and asked a question back, while checking the badge and walking to the desk by herself.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel when Gopika asks about his volunteering?
qa.a: He probably feels his effort was welcomed, glad that speaking to a stranger was met warmly.

grounding: Shows a person sitting alone at a festival feeling relief mixed with wariness when greeted by a stranger, and replying warmly with a question back.

passage: At the community library's story corner, Uma was telling Baljeet Aunty about her new sandals. "And they have a flower here, and when I walk they—" Through the window she saw the ice-cream cart. She was gone mid-sentence. Baljeet Aunty waited until Uma came back for her bag. "Uma, when you want to go, you can say, 'I'm going now, bye!' Then I know." Uma thought. "I'm going now, bye!" she tried. "Bye, Uma! Tell me about the flower next time." On Saturday, when her mother came, Uma said it all by herself before she ran.

qa.q: What did Uma see through the window?
qa.a: She saw the ice-cream cart.

qa.q: Why did Uma run off mid-sentence?
qa.a: She got so excited about the ice-cream cart that she forgot she was talking; she wasn't trying to be rude.

qa.q: What did Baljeet Aunty do that taught Uma a new skill?
qa.a: She gave Uma simple words, "I'm going now, bye!", let her try them, and said a warm goodbye back 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Baljeet Aunty when Uma ran off?
qa.a: She may have felt a little cut off and amused, left mid-sentence about the sandals.

grounding: Shows a young child running off mid-sentence and an adult modelling a simple goodbye she can use next time.

passage: In the boarding school's phone room, Tarun had been on the call with Gargi Nani for fourteen minutes, and three boys were waiting. "And then in maths, and also, Nani, the food is okay but the dal is watery, and—" Behind him, Rehaan sighed loudly. Tarun wanted to stop but didn't know how. Every time Nani said, "Accha, beta," he started a new story, because hanging up felt rude. The house parent on duty tore a slip from a notepad, wrote something and held it up: "Okay Nani, I have to go now. Love you. Talk on Sunday." Tarun read it out word for word. Nani laughed. "Go, go! Sunday." He put the phone down, surprised it had been that easy.

qa.q: How long had Tarun been on the call?
qa.a: He had been on the call for fourteen minutes.

qa.q: Why did Tarun keep starting new stories?
qa.a: He wanted to stop but felt hanging up would be rude, so he felt stuck and a bit anxious with the boys waiting.

qa.q: What words helped Tarun close the call?
qa.a: "Okay Nani, I have to go now. Love you. Talk on Sunday.", a clear signal followed by a warm close.

qa.q: How did Gargi Nani take the goodbye?
qa.a: She laughed and said, "Go, go! Sunday," so she clearly didn't feel hurt.

grounding: Shows a child unable to end a phone call with a grandparent until given a clear signal and a warm closing line.

passage:

Madhav: so how'd you escape 😅

Parul: and smiled and went
Madhav: and he was ok??
Parul: he said "Totally, go before the samosas vanish" 😄
Parul: and just now he sent me the trek photos he was talking about

qa.q: Who did Parul want to see before she left?

qa.q: How did Parul feel about ending the chat with Nishant's cousin?

qa.q: What could Madhav try instead of "ok bye"?

passage:
Monday. Yogesh was halfway through his idea for the client dashboard when Tejas glanced at his phone, said, "Okay, cool," and walked off. Yogesh stood in the corridor holding his half-sentence. He spent the afternoon wondering if the idea was stupid.
Wednesday. Tejas did it again at the coffee machine. This time Yogesh felt his jaw tighten, and he didn't bring the idea up at the stand-up.
Friday. Tejas's phone buzzed mid-conversation. He looked at it, then back at Yogesh. "Sorry, it's the client, I have to take this. I want to hear the rest, though. Four o'clock?" At four he came to Yogesh's desk with two cups of tea. Yogesh noticed how different the same interruption felt.

qa.q: What time did Tejas suggest on Friday?
qa.a: He suggested four o'clock.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel after Monday's cut-off?
qa.a: He felt dismissed and unsure, left holding his half-sentence and wondering all afternoon if the idea was stupid.

qa.q: What changed on Friday that softened the interruption?
qa.a: Tejas gave a reason, said he wanted to hear the rest, named a time and came back with tea.

qa.q: What might Tejas not have realised on Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: He may not have noticed that his quick "Okay, cool" left Yogesh feeling his idea didn't matter.

grounding: Shows a person feeling dismissed when a colleague ends a chat mid-thought with a glance at his phone, and how a promise to continue softens it.

passage:
Tuesday. Saurabh from the next flat caught Irawati at the lift with his theory about the water tank. Forty-five minutes later she was still nodding, and she had missed her sister's video call.
Thursday. He started again on the stairs. Irawati kept edging upward one step at a time, feeling rude and trapped the whole while.
Sunday. At the gate it began: "About the tank, the real problem is the society committee—" After a few minutes Irawati touched his sleeve lightly. "Saurabh-ji, so the real issue is the committee not checking the pipes. Thank you, that's useful. I have to go and cook now; I have guests at one." He blinked, then smiled. "Of course, of course. Go!" She walked upstairs feeling lighter, and he waved from the gate.

qa.q: Whose video call did Irawati miss on Tuesday?
qa.a: She missed her sister's video call.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel edging up the stairs on Thursday?
qa.a: She felt rude and trapped the whole time, unable to end the talk.

qa.q: Why did Irawati's Sunday ending work?
qa.a: She summed up his point, thanked him and named what she had to do next, so he felt heard and could let her go.

qa.q: How did Saurabh take being interrupted on Sunday?
qa.a: He smiled and said, "Of course, go!", so he didn't feel insulted, probably because his point had been summed up and thanked.

grounding: Shows a listener learning to end a long-winded neighbour's talk kindly with a summary, a thank-you and a clear next task.

passage:
"Duck! Duck! Splash!" Chandrika jabbed at the photo on the phone.
"Yes, the duck went splash in the pond," said Elizabeth Ammachi.
"Me... bread. Duck eat!"
"You gave the duck bread, and the duck ate it."
"Then... big dog! Woof! Me run!"
"A big dog barked, and you ran to Appa."
Chandrika nodded hard. "Appa up!"
"Appa picked you up. What a day at the park."
"Again!" said Chandrika, and started from the duck.

qa.q: What did Chandrika give the duck?
qa.a: She gave the duck bread.

qa.q: How did Chandrika seem to feel while retelling the park story?
qa.a: She seemed excited and proud 😊 jabbing at the photo, nodding hard and asking to tell it again.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth Ammachi doing that helped Chandrika's words grow?
qa.a: She echoed each fragment back as a full sentence, giving Chandrika the words for what happened.

qa.q: What might Appa feel if he heard this retelling?
qa.a: He would probably feel warm and amused that the dog and his picking her up had become part of her story.

grounding: Shows a toddler retelling a park visit in fragments while a grandmother echoes them back as full sentences.

passage:
"Papa! A dog chased me today. It was as big as a bus!"
"As big as a bus?" Kamal put down his newspaper. "Did it have wheels?"
"No! It had six legs and red eyes!"
"Wow. What did you do?"
"I flew! Up to the water tank."
Kamal laughed. "Brilliant story. Now tell me the true part. Was there a real dog?"
Charu twisted her frock. "A brown dog by the gate. It barked. I ran to Dadi."
"Good thing you ran to Dadi. And the flying?"
"...That was a story part."
"Best story part," Kamal said. "Draw me the six-legged one?"

qa.q: Where did Charu run when the brown dog barked?
qa.a: She ran to Dadi.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling when the real dog barked?
qa.a: She was probably scared, which may be why her story made the dog huge and let her fly away.

qa.q: How did Kamal keep a gentle line on the facts?
qa.a: He enjoyed the story, then asked for "the true part", so Charu could tell what really happened without being called a liar.

qa.q: How did Kamal seem to feel about Charu's tall tale?
qa.a: He seemed amused and delighted, calling it a brilliant story and asking for a drawing.

grounding: Shows a young child telling a tall tale about a huge dog and a parent enjoying it while gently asking for the true part.

passage: Kashish, you want the story again? All right, sit. The night you were born, the rain would not stop and the whole mohalla lost power. Your Nanaji, this same stubborn man, put a torch between his teeth and cycled through knee-deep water to fetch the nurse from Station Road. Twice he fell. Twice he got up. When he came back, soaked like a rat, you were already crying loud enough for the neighbours to cheer. He laughed so hard the torch fell into the bucket. That's why we say you arrived in a hurry and were loved by someone who would not give up. Your Aditi Nani has told you twenty times, and I'll tell you twenty more, because this story is yours.

qa.q: What did Nanaji hold between his teeth?
qa.a: He held a torch between his teeth.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel each time Nani tells this story?
qa.a: Kashish probably feels warm and proud, hearing again about arriving in a hurry and being loved by someone who would not give up.

qa.q: Which choice in the story shows who Nanaji was?
qa.a: Getting up after falling twice and cycling on through the water to fetch the nurse shows he would not give up.

qa.q: How might Nanaji have felt when he came back soaked and heard the baby crying?
qa.a: He was likely relieved and overjoyed, laughing so hard the torch fell into the bucket.

grounding: Shows a grandmother retelling the story of a child's birth night, giving the child a place and a sense of belonging in the family.
